report:
## Report: Does Soursop Cure Cancer?

**Short answer: No — this claim is not supported by reliable evidence.** Soursop (also called graviola, *Annona muricata*) is widely promoted online as a natural cancer cure, but the science does not support that claim in humans.

**What the evidence actually shows:**
- Laboratory (test-tube) and animal studies have found that soursop extracts and their active compounds, called acetogenins, can kill certain cancer cells and slow tumor growth in cell cultures ([Cancer Research UK](https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola); [PMC review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9497149/)). These are preliminary, mechanistic findings — not proof of a cure.
- **No clinical trials have shown soursop cures or effectively treats cancer in humans.** Major medical authorities — Memorial Sloan Kettering, Cancer Research UK, WebMD's medical review, and independent fact-checkers (PolitiFact, AFP Fact Check, Snopes, Africa Check) — all state there is insufficient or no reliable human evidence ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/); [PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/); [WebMD](https://www.webmd.com/cancer/graviola-cancer-overview)).
- One small double-blind safety trial in colorectal cancer patients tested a graviola extract only for toxicity, not effectiveness, over 8 weeks — it was not designed to test whether it treats cancer.
- **Safety concern:** The same acetogenin compounds (notably annonacin) that show anticancer activity in labs are also linked to neurotoxicity — specifically an atypical, levodopa-resistant Parkinsonism observed in Caribbean populations with high soursop/Annonaceae consumption ([Wikipedia: Annonacin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annonacin); PubMed study on mitochondrial toxicity).

**Bottom line:** Soursop contains bioactive compounds worth studying, but claiming it "cures cancer" in humans is unsupported and potentially risky, especially if it delays proven treatment or is consumed in high doses due to neurotoxicity concerns. It should not replace conventional cancer therapy.
